extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, postdocs, junior faculty, and aspiring academic mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: General, stage-by-stage career advice for people pursuing an academic career in mathematics, covering undergraduate through postdoctoral concerns plus time-management and presentation skills. The page collects concise heuristics and links to more detailed treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choosing schools, advisors, or directions primarily for prestige; evaluate fit, mentorship, and long-term prospects instead. (See related subpage 'don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Study at different places
rubrics_metrics.description: But you should study at different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience different institutions/environments during training to broaden perspective and networks; diversity of training can be beneficial for development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value more than grades/exams
rubrics_metrics.description: There is more to maths than grades and exams and methods; there is also more to maths than rigour and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate problem-solving ability, intuition, exposition and broader mathematical understanding rather than focusing solely on coursework grades or rote proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work hard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to work hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained effort is a core ingredient of research progress; combine with professional habits (see next items) rather than relying on bursts of inspiration alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work professionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Work professionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professional standards: meet deadlines, communicate clearly, keep good records, and behave reliably with collaborators and mentors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy your work
rubrics_metrics.description: But it is also important to enjoy your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek intrinsic satisfaction; long-term productivity and creativity are aided by genuine interest and enjoyment in the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think ahead and ask dumb questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Think ahead to understand the way forward; ask yourself dumb questions to understand the way before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan research trajectories and clarify goals; asking basic ('dumb') questions can reveal misunderstandings and illuminate simpler routes forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend talks and conferences, even those not directly related to your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to diverse topics stimulates ideas, builds networks, and helps you learn how to present and hear mathematics in different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your advisor
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to your advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular communication with your advisor helps align expectations, get feedback, and navigate career decisions; leverage their experience and contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take the initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: But also take the initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be proactive about finding problems, collaborators, talks, and opportunities rather than waiting for direction; balance deference to advisors with independent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t prematurely obsess on a single big problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t prematurely obsess on a single “big problem” or “big theory”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid putting all effort into one grand aim too early; diversify projects to build skills, produce publishable results, and avoid wasted long-term investment on avenues that stall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down what you’ve done and make it available
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down what you’ve done, and make your work available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep clear written records, prepare notes/papers, share preprints or technical reports; making work accessible increases impact and feedback opportunities. (See linked advice on how to write and submit papers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field; learn outside it
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and relearn your field, but don’t be afraid to learn things outside your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously refresh core knowledge while acquiring new neighboring skills; cross-disciplinary learning can provide tools and perspectives that open new research directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand tool limitations and other tools’ power; aim just beyond current range
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the limitations of your tools, but also learn the power of other mathematician’s tools. In particular, you should continually aim just beyond your current range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know what techniques can and cannot do; study others’ methods to expand your toolkit; choose problems slightly beyond current comfort to grow capability without overreaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible and patient in research
rubrics_metrics.description: In your research, be both flexible and patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust approaches as new information arrives and tolerate slow progress on difficult problems; balance persistence with willingness to pivot to more tractable or productive directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and present research; be considerate of audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You should definitely travel and present your research if given the opportunity. But be considerate of your audience; talks are not the same as papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conferences and visits to disseminate work and get feedback; tailor talks to the audience level, emphasize intuition and narrative in talks versus formal detail in papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of your own work and use the wastebasket
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sceptical of your own work, and don’t be afraid to use the wastebasket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate your ideas and drop lines of attack that are unpromising; discarding partial work is productive and prevents time sink on doomed approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batch low-intensity tasks together
rubrics_metrics.description: Batch low-intensity tasks together to take advantage of economies of scale and to reduce distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group administrative/low-focus tasks to reduce context switching and protect deep-work time for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn how to write and submit papers
rubrics_metrics.description: In this regard, I have some advice on how to write and submit papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop skills in exposition, selecting appropriate journals, preparing clear submissions and responses to referees; dissemination is part of professional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build your own network of colleagues and collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Build your own network of colleagues and collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively cultivate collaborations, mentorships, and a community; networks provide problem ideas, feedback, and professional opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a plan but remain willing to change it
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t jump in blind. Have a plan so that you have some kind of structure but at the same time, don’t worry if you have to stray from that plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a roadmap for training and career milestones while retaining flexibility to adapt as interests or circumstances change; avoid dogmatic adherence to plans that make you unhappy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer good institutional/advising fit; try to go to the best place you can
rubrics_metrics.description: Go to the best place you can; at a good place, if your relationship with your advisor doesn’t work out there will be other reputable people to work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, choose institutions with strong research groups and multiple potential mentors to reduce dependency on a single advisor and increase exposure to leading work; beware fast-moving 'flashy' fields where being close to leaders matters.
